# Getting Started in Positron

> **Prompt 1.** Download and Install Positron. As you watch the videos in Step 1 through Step 4, follow the activities in the video and be familiar with Positron.

Working on this reflection helped me understand how the project folder, the Quarto source, and the finished report fit together. The **Explorer** keeps the report and supporting files visible, the **Source Editor** is where I can change the YAML options, and the **Console** gives me a place to try a line of R before putting it into a report. The **Variables** pane is useful when I need to check what an object contains after running code.

1. Open the `Intro-Positron` folder as the project workspace.
2. Create and save the `.qmd` file with the author, HTML format, and table-of-contents options in YAML.
3. Render the file and open the HTML in a browser. Check the headings, table of contents, and links from a reader’s point of view.

::: {.callout-tip}
The **Render** step matters because the instructor will primarily read the HTML. For example, changing a heading in my source also means checking that it appears at the right level in the rendered table of contents.
:::

# Comparing Positron and RStudio

> **Prompt 2.** Based on what you learned from Step 1 through Step 4, what do you like about Positron compared with RStudio?

RStudio’s layout feels familiar for an assignment that uses only R. What I like about Positron is how easily I can move between organizing files, inspecting data, and writing the report. For a marketing analytics project, I might clean a dataset in Python and then summarize the results in an R-based Quarto report. Keeping those files in the same workspace makes it easier to trace a result back to the code that produced it.

The comparison in @tbl-ide focuses on tasks that matter to me when preparing an assignment.

| Task | What I like about Positron | What I value in RStudio |
|---|---|---|
| Inspect data | I can move from the Variables pane into Data Explorer to check fields and values. | The Environment pane gives me a familiar view of objects in an R session. |
| Navigate project files | The Explorer and Command Palette make it easy to switch between source files, terminal commands, and Git. | The RStudio project layout is familiar for a smaller R assignment. |
| Write reports | I can keep R and Python scripts alongside the Quarto report in the same workspace. | I can use the Quarto workflow I already know for an R report. |

: Positron and RStudio in my coursework. {#tbl-ide}

# Using AI in Positron

> **Prompt 3.** In Step 4, the video demonstrates how you can use AI.

## Ways to use AI

> **Prompt 3.1.** Describe the various ways you can use AI inside Positron. Some are free while others are not.

Inline completions can suggest the next line while I type. **Posit Assistant** chat is better suited to explaining an error, suggesting a debugging step, or helping me understand a Quarto option. Provider choice affects the features and cost. Some services offer free access or limited free tiers, while others require a subscription or charge for API usage. Verified students can activate GitHub Copilot Student through GitHub Education.[^ai-access]

[^ai-access]: See the [Positron provider guide](https://positron.posit.co/assistant-providers.html) and [GitHub’s Copilot Student instructions](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-on-github/set-up-copilot/enable-copilot/set-up-for-students).

## Tools and practical use

> **Prompt 3.2.** Which AI tools have you installed or set up? Which AI tools did you find beneficial for you?

The two features I would use most are inline completion for syntax and chat for troubleshooting. For example, if a Quarto table does not appear in the report, I would ask chat to explain the render message and identify the first thing to check. I would then change one setting at a time and render again so I can tell which change fixed the problem.

::: {.callout-note}
My in-editor AI setup and hands-on test have yet to be documented.
:::

## GitHub Education and Copilot

> **Prompt 3.3.** I strongly recommend using GitHub Copilot, which is free if you apply for an education account.
>
> 1. Apply for it and take a screenshot showing you were accepted into the education program.
> 2. Play with it and do you find it helpful or distracting? Please elaborate.

**GitHub Education verification.** An approval screenshot is pending.

<!-- When available, replace the preceding line with the actual evidence:
![GitHub Education approval](github-education-accepted.png){#fig-education fig-alt="GitHub Education approval confirmation"}
-->

**What I would look for in a hands-on test.** I would give Copilot a small task I can check myself, such as calculating a survey response rate. A suggestion is helpful if it speeds up the syntax while using the correct denominator. It becomes distracting when it offers a longer function than the task requires or invites me to accept the calculation before checking missing values. I would use chat when I need an explanation of the denominator and limit inline suggestions when I am still thinking through the analysis.

In this example, 18 completed surveys out of 24 invitations give a response rate of 75%. I can verify that result by hand before comparing it with any suggestion.

<details class="code-fold">
<summary>Show R example</summary>

```r
completed_surveys <- 18
invited_people <- 24
response_rate <- completed_surveys / invited_people
round(100 * response_rate, digits = 1)
```

</details>

# Publishing to GitHub Pages

> **Prompt 4.** Publish this report to GitHub Pages.
>
> Note that although both GitHub Pages and the GitHub repo are online, they are different. GitHub Pages is a website publishing service that hosts the rendered HTML from a QMD file.

The **GitHub repository** holds the editable Quarto source and tracks changes. **GitHub Pages** gives the instructor a URL to read the rendered report in a browser. With `embed-resources: true`, the HTML can also be opened as a standalone file.

The publishing setup uses the rendered report as `index.html` in the root of the `main` branch. In **Settings → Pages**, the publishing source is that branch and folder. The Pages link in the appendix opens the web version once deployment is complete.
